questions.q: What is at the centre of our solar system?
options: The Sun, which is a star
questions.explain: The Sun, a star, is at the centre of the solar system. The eight planets, dwarf planets and their moons orbit it.

questions.q: What is the first stage in the life cycle of a star?
options: A nebula (cloud of dust and gas) collapsing into a protostar
questions.explain: A star begins as a nebula. Gravity pulls the dust and gas together to form a protostar, which heats up until nuclear fusion of hydrogen begins, forming a main sequence star.

questions.q: For an object in a circular orbit, in which direction does the gravitational force act?
options: Towards the centre of the orbit, acting as the centripetal force
Away from the centre of the orbit
There is no force on an orbiting object
questions.explain: Gravity acts towards the centre of the orbit, providing the centripetal force that keeps the object moving in a circle and constantly changing direction.

questions.q: What is observed in the light from distant galaxies?
questions.explain: Light from distant galaxies is red-shifted — its wavelength is increased (shifted towards the red end). This shows the galaxies are moving away from us.

questions.q: How did the Sun form?
options: From a collapsing cloud of dust and gas (a nebula) pulled together by gravity
From the explosion of a planet
From a black hole running out of energy
questions.explain: The Sun formed when a cloud of dust and gas (nebula) was pulled together by gravity. As it collapsed it heated up, eventually starting nuclear fusion.

questions.q: What makes a main sequence star (like the Sun) stable for billions of years?
options: There are no forces acting on it
The inward force of gravity is balanced by the outward pressure from fusion energy
It is held together by magnetism
questions.explain: During the main sequence the inward pull of gravity is balanced by the outward force from the expansion of hot gases (energy released by hydrogen fusion). This equilibrium keeps the star stable.

questions.q: An object moves at a steady speed in a circular orbit. Why is it still accelerating?
options: Its direction (and therefore velocity) is constantly changing
It is moving in a straight line
questions.explain: Velocity is a vector. Even at constant speed, the direction is continuously changing in a circular orbit, so the velocity changes — this change in velocity is the (centripetal) acceleration.

questions.q: How does the red-shift of a galaxy relate to its distance from Earth?
options: More distant galaxies have a smaller red-shift
More distant galaxies have a larger red-shift, showing they recede faster
Red-shift is the same for all galaxies
questions.explain: The more distant a galaxy, the greater its red-shift, meaning it is moving away faster. This is evidence that the whole universe is expanding.

questions.q: Which of these correctly describes our solar system?
options: One star, eight planets, plus dwarf planets and moons
Only the Sun and the Earth
questions.explain: Our solar system contains one star (the Sun), eight planets, several dwarf planets (such as Pluto) and many moons (natural satellites).

questions.q: What will happen to the Sun (a low-mass star) when it runs low on hydrogen fuel?
options: It will explode as a supernova
It will expand into a red giant, then become a white dwarf
It will become a black hole
It will become a neutron star
questions.explain: A low-mass star like the Sun swells into a red giant, then sheds its outer layers and the core becomes a white dwarf that slowly cools.

questions.q: For a stable orbit, if a satellite moves to a larger orbital radius, what must happen to its speed?
options: Its speed stays exactly the same
It cannot stay in orbit at a larger radius
questions.explain: For a stable orbit at a given radius there is only one possible speed. A larger orbital radius requires a slower orbital speed; a smaller radius requires a faster speed.

questions.q: The observation that distant galaxies are all receding, and faster the further away they are, is evidence for which theory?
options: The Big Bang theory — the universe began from a small dense point and is expanding
That the Earth is at the exact centre of a static universe
questions.explain: An expanding universe in which distant galaxies recede faster is strong evidence for the Big Bang theory: the universe began from a very small, hot, dense region and has been expanding ever since.

questions.q: What keeps the planets in orbit around the Sun?
options: The gravitational force of attraction from the Sun
questions.explain: Gravity provides the force that keeps planets in orbit. The Sun's large mass produces a gravitational attraction acting on each planet.

questions.q: Put the correct end-of-life path for a HIGH-mass star in order.
options: Red giant → white dwarf → black hole
Red super giant → supernova → neutron star or black hole
Red super giant → white dwarf → neutron star
questions.explain: A high-mass star becomes a red super giant, then explodes as a supernova. The remaining core becomes a neutron star, or a black hole if the star was massive enough.

questions.q: What does CMBR (cosmic microwave background radiation) provide evidence for?
questions.explain: The cosmic microwave background radiation is low-level microwave radiation found across all of space. It is best explained as the leftover 'afterglow' of the Big Bang, which only the Big Bang theory predicts.

questions.q: Which of these is a NATURAL satellite?
questions.explain: The Moon is a natural satellite of the Earth. Communications satellites, GPS satellites and the ISS are artificial (man-made) satellites.

questions.q: Where are elements heavier than iron formed?
options: In the cores of low-mass main sequence stars
questions.explain: Fusion in stars produces elements up to iron. Elements heavier than iron are formed in the huge energies of a supernova explosion, which then scatters them into space.

questions.q: Why did scientists propose the existence of dark matter and dark energy?
options: To explain the colour of stars
To explain observations (such as galaxy motion and accelerating expansion) that ordinary matter alone cannot account for
To replace the Big Bang theory
Because the universe contains no ordinary matter
questions.explain: Observations of how galaxies move and how the universe's expansion is speeding up cannot be explained by visible matter alone, so scientists proposed dark matter and dark energy. There is still much we do not understand about them.

questions.q: What is a supernova?
options: The birth of a new star from a nebula
The explosion of a massive star at the end of its life
questions.explain: A supernova is the violent explosion of a high-mass star (red super giant) at the end of its life, scattering elements into space and leaving a neutron star or black hole.

questions.q: A spectral line normally at one wavelength is observed at a LONGER wavelength in a galaxy's light. What does this tell us about the galaxy?
options: It is moving away from us (receding)
It is stationary relative to us
questions.explain: A shift to longer wavelength is a red-shift, which means the source is moving away from us. The bigger the shift, the faster it recedes.

questions.q: Which remnant is left when the core of an extremely massive star collapses so much that not even light can escape?
questions.explain: If the collapsing core after a supernova is massive enough, it forms a black hole, whose gravity is so strong that not even light can escape. Less massive cores leave a neutron star.

questions.q: During the main sequence stage, what process releases energy in a star's core?
options: Burning of fuel like a fire (combustion)
Nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium
questions.explain: Main sequence stars release energy by nuclear fusion, joining hydrogen nuclei to form helium. This is not chemical burning — it is a nuclear process in the core.
